newsitem.title: KENYA: Student protest briefly disrupts Kenyan capital.
newsitem.headline: Student protest briefly disrupts Kenyan capital.

text.p: Students demanding constitutional reforms and the departure from office of President Daniel arap Moi briefly seized control of a main highway in Kenya's capital Nairobi on Tuesday, witnesses said.
But by 11 a.m. (0800 GMT) traffic was normal again on Haile Selassie Avenue, where hundreds of students from Kenya Polytechnic had erected barricades, chanting "Moi must go. We want reforms."
"The students came out again this morning, but now they have gone back. It was not serious," said a taxi driver on the avenue.
In Mombasa, Moslem preacher Sheikh Balala, a fierce critic of Moi, said he would tour the city and visit schools on Tuesday after returning from two years in exile, witnesses said.
Balala returned to Kenya on Saturday from exile in Germany vowing to spearhead a reform campaign.
"I don't recognise the forthcoming elections and I would rather voters burned their registration cards," Balala told a crowd of around 1,000 at the Sakina Mosque in the Indian Ocean port.
But his aides said a planned "illegal" rally in Mombasa on Tuesday had been called off.
Nine people were killed last week in the most serious civil disturbances since a 1990 campaign to press for constitutional reforms that led to the introduction of a multi-party system.
Opposition-backed groups have campaigned since April for reforms before presidential and parliamentary elections due this year. No date has been set for the polls.

Authorities shut Kenya Polytechnic late on Monday after clashes between some 3,000 students and police on Haile Selassie Avenue. The students defied the closure order and turned up for classes on Tuesday.
The clashes did not affect most commerce or traffic in Nairobi, unlike unrest last week.

Political analysts say reforms would reduce the power of Moi, 73 and in office since 1978. But he is widely expected to win elections against an opposition that has built a fragile cohesion based on demands for reform.
The Polytechnic students said they were in solidarity with their university colleagues and were backing growing calls for constitutional reforms.
The government shut the country's two main universities last week after students, heeding opposition demands for reforms, battled police and paramilitary forces.
Authorities ordered Nairobi University and Jomo Kenyatta University closed indefinitely last week and students were sent home following days of clashes with riot police in the capital.
Five people -- two students, two passers-by and a journalist -- were hurt on Monday as police wielding batons and firing live ammunition and teargas moved onto the Polytechnic campus.
The students were protesting against a new bill that provided for expulsion for non-payment of fees and revised charges for exams. They also demanded constitutional reform.
Fourteen people were arrested during the disturbances and would be charged on Tuesday, police said.

Moi said last Friday he would take action against any attempt to bring chaos to the country and challenged the opposition to take the debate on reforms to parliament, where his ruling party has a majority.
